text: Masking policies change what a role sees inside a cell. A row access policy does something different — it decides whether an entire row is visible at all.

Instead of hardcoding role names into the policy itself, this pattern uses a real table — a mapping of role to city permissions. One row says tb_test_role can see Tokyo. Adding a new role later is an insert, not a policy rewrite.

Here's the policy itself — a boolean expression. A row passes if the querying role is a privileged bypass role, or if the mapping table has a row proving that role can see this particular city. ALTER TABLE ADD ROW ACCESS POLICY is what actually attaches it, naming which column the policy checks.

Querying the table as the restricted role — every single row comes back as Tokyo, nowhere else. And notice the names are masked here too — row access and masking are independent mechanisms stacking on the same table.
Same as masking, a row access policy travels downstream automatically. This view spans every city in the base table, but grouped by city and queried by the restricted role, only Tokyo shows up.
Next lesson: secure views — hiding not just rows or values, but the view's own definition from anyone who shouldn't see how it works.
